note: Ops vocabulary for --explain (sidebar): matcher injects at most 3 one-liners into goal-blind prompts on deterministic match; each def <=140 chars (~35 tokens). Never auto-loaded whole.

terms.def: Cap how many requests a client can make in a window; excess gets throttled or rejected to protect the service.
Store reusable results close to the reader so repeat requests skip recomputation or refetching.
Spread incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single one is overwhelmed.
A server in front of app servers that forwards client requests, often adding TLS termination and caching.
Single entry point for API traffic handling routing, auth, rate limits, and request shaping.
Automated pipelines that build, test, and deploy code on every change.
Container runtime packaging an app with its dependencies into a portable, isolated image.
Orchestrator that schedules, scales, and heals containerized workloads across machines.
Mechanism for services to find each other's live addresses as instances come and go.
Fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy, pausing calls briefly instead of piling up doomed requests.
Maximum wait for an operation; exceeding it aborts so one slow call can't freeze the system.
Re-attempt a failed operation, ideally only for transient failures and with backoff.
Retry delays that double (plus jitter) to avoid hammering a struggling service.
Repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once; what makes retries safe.
Buffers holding tasks or events for async processing, decoupling producers from consumers.
Publishers broadcast to topics and subscribers receive matches, without direct coupling.
Design where components react to emitted events rather than calling each other directly.
Operations spanning services or databases that must all succeed or all roll back; hard to get right.
Long transaction split into local steps with compensating actions that undo prior steps on failure.
Holding area for messages that repeatedly fail processing, kept for inspection and replay.
Scheduled tasks that run automatically at fixed times or intervals.
Persistent two-way connections for real-time client-server messaging over one socket.
Client holds a request open until the server has new data or times out, then immediately re-requests.
One-way server-to-client event stream over HTTP for live updates without polling.
Auxiliary structures letting the database find rows without scanning whole tables.
Rewriting and tuning queries (and indexes) so the database executes them efficiently.
Anti-pattern fetching one row then N follow-ups in a loop instead of one batched query.
Reusing a fixed set of open database connections instead of opening one per request.
Read-only database copies absorbing read traffic to relieve the primary.
Splitting data horizontally across databases by key to scale writes and storage.
Dividing a table into smaller segments for performance and manageability.
Copying data to multiple nodes for redundancy, availability, or read scaling.
Process by which distributed nodes agree on one coordinator or primary.
A distributed store can fully guarantee only two of consistency, availability, partition tolerance.
Replicas may briefly disagree but converge to the same value when writes stop.
Assume no conflicts; verify at write time via version check and retry on clash.
Lock the record before working so nobody else can touch it until done.
Mutual exclusion across machines so only one node acts at a time.
Bugs where the outcome depends on the timing or order of concurrent operations.
Two or more operations each waiting on a lock the other holds, freezing both forever.
Allocated memory never released, growing usage until slowdown or crash.
Runtime automatically reclaiming memory the program no longer references.
Code that behaves correctly when multiple threads use it concurrently.
Slow consumers signaling producers to ease off, preventing overload and unbounded queues.
Automatically adding or removing capacity based on load metrics.
Adding more machines or instances to handle load (scaling out).
Bigger machine (CPU/RAM) for a single instance (scaling up).
Geographically distributed cache network serving content from near the user.
Caching responses at edge locations close to users to cut latency.
Removing or refreshing stale cached entries when source data changes; famously hard.
Toggles enabling or disabling behavior at runtime without redeploying.
Run old and new environments; switch traffic over, roll back by switching back.
Roll out to a small user subset first, expand only if healthy.
Replace instances gradually in batches, keeping the service up throughout.
Reverting to the previous known-good version after a bad deploy.
Endpoints or probes reporting whether a service instance can serve traffic.
Liveness restarts dead containers; readiness gates traffic until an instance is ready.
Continuously watching system health, performance, and errors.
Recording timestamped event records for debugging, auditing, and analysis.
Following one request across service hops with correlated trace and span IDs.
Numeric measurements over time (counts, latencies, gauges) for dashboards and alerts.
Automated notifications when a metric crosses a threshold.
Service-level objectives: promised reliability targets, e.g. 99.9% success over 30 days.
Service-level indicators: the measured numbers an SLO target is set against.
Allowed failure room (100% minus SLO); spending it fast means slow down releases.
Understanding internals from external signals: logs, metrics, and traces together.
Storing credentials in dedicated vaults or services, never in code or chat.
Identity and access management: who or what can do which actions on which resources.
Delegated authorization letting apps act for a user without seeing their password.
Regularly replacing tokens (short-lived access, rotated refresh) to limit stolen-token damage.
Encrypted transport authenticating servers and protecting data in flight.
Encrypting stored data so stolen disks or backups don't expose it.
Encrypting data while it moves over networks.
Web application firewall filtering malicious HTTP traffic before it reaches the app.
Absorbing or blocking distributed denial-of-service floods to stay reachable.
Browser mechanism where servers declare which origins may call them cross-origin.
Attack tricking a logged-in browser into unwanted actions; mitigated with tokens.
Attack smuggling SQL through inputs; prevented with parameterized queries.
Attack injecting scripts into pages others view; prevented by escaping output.
Attack making the server request attacker-chosen internal URLs; allow-list destinations.
Versioned scripts evolving the schema safely across deploys.
Numbering schema changes so code and database stay compatible.
Plans and drills to restore service after catastrophic failure.
Restorable copies of data and systems, tested regularly.
Automatically shifting traffic or work to a standby when the primary fails.
Running in several regions for latency, resilience, and compliance.
Deliberately injecting failures to verify resilience before reality does.
Rightsizing resources and cutting waste; cheapest adequate tier always.
Latency when a serverless function initializes on first use after idling.
Platform caps on runtime, memory, payload, and concurrency.
Time for one operation or request to complete, end to end.
Operations completed per unit time; capacity under sustained load.
The latency 99% of requests beat; the near-worst case users feel.
Slow outliers that dominate user pain in fan-out systems.
Network splits isolating groups of nodes from each other.
Disagreement between machine clocks, breaking ordering and expiry.
Name resolution mapping hostnames to IPs; TTLs govern propagation delays.
Reliable ordered streams versus best-effort datagrams; pick by need.
Newer HTTP with multiplexing and QUIC transport for faster transfers.
High-performance RPC over HTTP/2 with schema-first contracts.
Event callbacks: a service POSTs to your URL when something happens.
Evolving APIs without breaking clients, with deprecation windows.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking vs feature vs fix, for predictable upgrades.
Defining infrastructure in versioned files instead of console clicks.
IaC tool declaring cloud resources; plans changes before applying.
Packaged Kubernetes manifests with templated values for repeatable deploys.
Reusing unchanged build steps and artifacts to make rebuilds fast.
Conflicting transitive version requirements making installs painful.
Live degradations handled via triage, mitigation, fix, then postmortem.
Rotation responding to alerts and incidents, with escalation paths.
Blameless reviews after incidents capturing causes and follow-ups.
